issue.issue_text: Whether the short story 'Shama' is obscene and offends the provisions of Section 292 of the Indian Penal Code.

facts: The appellant, an author, wrote a short story titled 'Shama' which was published in a Marathi magazine.
The author and the publisher were convicted for obscenity under Section 292 of the Indian Penal Code by the High Court, which reversed an acquittal by the Magistrate.
The High Court identified specific passages in the story as being obscene.
The story's plot revolves around a poet, Nishikant, and his relationships, including two past painful affairs which are recalled as a deterrent to a new involvement.
law: The legal test for obscenity is whether a work, viewed as a whole, is likely to deprave and corrupt those whose minds are open to such influences and into whose hands the work is likely to fall.
The court must not judge isolated passages but must take an overall view of the entire work.
A balance must be struck between freedom of speech and public decency and morality. When the latter is substantially transgressed, the former must give way.
If art and obscenity are mixed, the art must preponderate to such an extent that it overshadows the obscenity, or the obscenity must be trivial and insignificant.
The work must be judged by contemporary national standards to determine if it panders to lascivious or prurient interests.
application: The Supreme Court analyzed the story 'Shama' in its entirety, not just the passages flagged by the High Court.
It determined that the story, read as a whole, was not pornography and did not pander to prurient interests. It noted that the story might lack high literary quality but was not obscene.
The Court found that the specific passages did not have the tendency to deprave or corrupt readers, including adolescents.
It reasoned that presenting situations with a strong moral lesson and condemning wrongful conduct, as the story did, does not corrupt morals.
The Court concluded that the story would not cause a class of readers to suffer a decline in their moral outlook or arouse impure thoughts.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the short story 'Shama' was not obscene under Section 292 of the Indian Penal Code. It found that the story, when viewed as a whole, did not have a tendency to deprave or corrupt its likely readers. Therefore, the Court allowed the appeal and set aside the conviction and fine.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the short story 'Shama' is obscene and offends the provisions of Section 292 of the Indian Penal Code.
appellant_arguments: The short story 'Shama' is not obscene and its passages do not pervert the morals of adolescents.
respondent_arguments: The short story 'Shama' is obscene and offends the provisions of Section 292 of the Indian Penal Code.

cases.case_name: Ranjit D. Udeshi v. State of Maharashtra
cases.principle: The legal test for determining what constitutes obscenity under Section 292 of the Indian Penal Code.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When determining obscenity, it is the duty of the Court to take an overall view of the entire work to determine whether the passages are so likely to deprave and corrupt those whose minds are open to such influences and in whose hands the work is likely to fall, and in doing so, the influence of the work on the social morality of contemporary society cannot be overlooked.
obiter: As the question of obscenity may have to be judged in the light of a claim that the work has pre-dominant literary merit, it may be necessary, if required, to rely to a certain extent on the evidence and views of leading litterateurs on that aspect.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Applying the test of viewing the work as a whole, the Court found that the impugned passages in the short story 'Shama' could not be considered obscene. The passages, which recalled the protagonist's two earlier painful love affairs, were contextualized as a 'repellant to any further involvement' and did not amount to pornography, nor did they contain descriptions of the sex act. Therefore, the Court concluded that the passages were not likely to deprave and corrupt the morals of adolescents or pander to lascivious, prurient, or sexually precocious minds.
legal_tests_applied: The test of obscenity is whether the tendency of the matter is to deprave and corrupt those whose minds are open to such immoral influences, and into whose hands a publication of this sort may fall.

It is the duty of the court to consider the obscene matter by taking an overall view of the entire work and to determine whether the obscene passages are so likely to deprave and corrupt those whose minds are open to such influences and in whose hands the book is likely to fall.
The influence of the book on the social morality of our contemporary society cannot be overlooked.
Where obscenity and art are mixed, art must so preponderate as to throw the obscenity into a shadow or the obscenity so trivial and insignificant that it can have no effect and may be overlooked.
The charge of obscenity must be judged from the aspect of whether a class, not an isolated case, into whose hands the book falls might suffer in their moral outlook or become depraved by reading it.

Treating with sex in a manner offensive to public decency and morality, judged by our national standards and considered likely to pander to lascivious, prurient or sexually precocious minds, must determine the result.
policy_considerations: A balance should be maintained between freedom of speech and expression and public decency and morality but when the latter is substantially transgressed the former must give way.
We need not attempt to bowdlerize all literature and thus rob speech and expression of freedom.
